Extremely Rude Owner, Poor Hygiene, and an Unacceptable Customer Experience!!!!!!

Today, we visited this restaurant as a group of 7 adults and 2 children to have some food and drinks. The waitress initially welcomed us and seated us, but what happened next was completely unacceptable.

A man sitting at the next table was feeding his dog. After a few minutes, he suddenly started shouting at us, repeatedly yelling, “Leave my restaurant!” and “Leave right now!” We were shocked and confused by his aggressive behavior, especially since we had two children with us who were frightened by the situation. We chose not to argue and simply wanted to avoid further confrontation.

There was absolutely NO REASON for this behavior. Everyone in our group was polite, respectful, and well-mannered. We had done nothing to provoke or upset anyone, so being shouted at and told to leave for no apparent reason was shocking and completely unacceptable.

The waitress later apologized and explained that the man was the owner of the restaurant. I was extremely disappointed that the owner himself treated customers in such a rude, intimidating, and unwelcoming manner.

I was also concerned about the hygiene standards, as I saw the dog eating from plates on the table. This raised serious concerns for me about food hygiene and cleanliness.

Thankfully, we had not started eating before this incident occurred. What should have been a pleasant family outing turned into a very unpleasant and stressful experience.

Based on my experience, I would not recommend this restaurant to anyone. The owner's behavior was unacceptable, and the situation left us feeling unwelcome and uncomfortable. Customer service and hygiene should be basic priorities for any restaurant, and unfortunately, this experience fell far short of my expectations.

I would give zero stars if that were an option. I will never return and would strongly advise others to consider this experience before visiting.

Response to the Owner’s Comment:

When we decided to sit at your restaurant, none of us knew that stepping outside briefly to grab something from the car would apparently be such a SERIOUS issue. At the time, we were still settling into our table, and none of us had even placed an order yet. Some members of our group simply went to the car to get something for the children. It was a simple, innocent reason, not an attempt to disrespect you or your restaurant.

Are your customers expected to remain at their tables once they sit down, without even being allowed to step outside briefly before ordering? And if a few people step away to get something from their car while the group is still settling in, does that give you the right to dismiss the entire group and treat everyone so rudely?

Instead of making assumptions or escalating the situation, you could have simply asked us what was happening. A little understanding and basic courtesy would have made all the difference.

Your response, “Game over,” says a lot about how you chose to handle the situation. We were a group of adults with children, and we expected nothing more than a reasonable level of courtesy and respect. We had not ordered anything, caused no disturbance, or done anything to justify being treated in such an AGGRESSIVE and UNWELCOMING manner.

This experience was disappointing, and your response has only reinforced my concerns about your approach to customer service. A little patience and respectful communication would have gone a long way.

review_text:
The service, music, ambiance, and food here are absolutely amazing! From the moment we walked in, the staff was incredibly friendly and attentive, making us feel welcome right away.
Their cocktail game is top-tier, the drinks are perfectly balanced with a creative twist. We started with a dirty martini, a mezcal penicillin, and a glass of wine, all of which were excellent. For appetizers, we ordered the crispy tuna fries and the hamachi. Both were incredibly fresh, but what really stands out is how unique the sauces are. Everything is prepared to absolute perfection.
For our main course, we split the duck adobo and the fried rice, and it did not disappoint. During dinner, Chef Josh actually came over to our table to talk to us. He shared the inspiration behind the menu, explaining his incredible fusion of French and Filipino culinary styles, and mentioned that his mentor worked with Jean-Georges for a long time. You can truly taste that world-class pedigree in every single bite.
I highly recommend coming to this restaurant for an unforgettable meal. Plus, if you are looking to keep the night going, they transition into a club after 10 PM. We will definitely be back!

I had this place on my hit list for a little bit and was finally able to stop in for a Friday dinner.

As soon as you get into the place, you realize the service is a team sport and we were assisted by the host who helped until our official server stopped by. The place is intimate, maybe 10-12 tables not including the bar.

The wine list is extensive and apparently if you want to get a bottle there’s a whole list from sister restaurant Parcelle. I ended up going with a Riesling that was available by the glass and was told it would go well with the spice of the dishes.

We ordered the cucumber and wood ear mushroom salad, the water spinach which was fresh and included a sauce that required dipping with the shake shake fries, got a complimentary salt and pepper fried tofu dish, the SPICY chili fried chicken with chili crisp glaze that I’m happy I had the Riesling to wash down but just wish came with a warning, the chicken sausage fried rice, the duck breast, and just because my friend wanted to see what the pastry chef could do, the sticky rice with mango.

Definitely too much food but I’m happy my friend took home the leftovers we weren’t able to finish.

Overall, a great dining experience until a party of 20 came in towards the end of our meal and caused my Apple Watch noise alarm to go off. Can’t be made about a celebration of friends on a weekend night in the city.

review_text:
The food at Corima is honestly wonderful: creative, surprising and, most importantly, really delicious. There were several dishes I absolutely loved, which is why I was a little sad that the overall experience didn’t quite feel like five stars to me. The food itself is the clear highlight, and I would genuinely love to return, especially to try the à la carte menu.

The tasting menu included some excellent and memorable dishes. However, I didn’t realise when booking through Resy that the tasting menu was the only option attached to our reservation. We weren’t shown a food menu or asked whether we preferred the tasting menu or à la carte. Later, I saw the couple next to us enjoying beautiful full-sized dishes and realised that à la carte was also available. Maybe I missed something while booking, but I really wish I had known, as their dinner looked like my dream meal. Personally, I would much rather have three amazing dishes and more than one bite of each than thirteen tiny courses.

Unfortunately, the service and communication sometimes felt less polished than I had expected. When we arrived, there was nobody at the entrance, so we — along with another couple — walked into the restaurant before eventually coming back to find someone.

I had also mentioned some food intolerances in my reservation and was told that the restaurant had tried several times to contact me by phone and email. I may have missed calls while travelling, but I never received an email. In the end, I explained that they were intolerances rather than allergies and that I could be flexible, so it wasn’t really an issue, it was just the communication side that felt a little odd.

There were also a few moments during the meal when clearer communication would have helped. We ordered the tortilla with caviar after seeing it at the table next to us. It arrived without caviar and without explanation. We asked again and ordered another one with caviar, but that one also arrived without it. Only when we asked a second time were we told that they had run out. Of course, restaurants run out of things, and that is absolutely no problem; I would simply have appreciated being told before the dish arrived twice.

Something similar happened when we asked to add one of the à la carte dishes we had seen at the neighbouring table. We made clear that we didn’t want to change the tasting menu, but simply wanted to add and pay for another dish. We were told that someone would check, but nobody came back to us. Once dessert arrived, we understood that it wasn’t happening.

None of these things individually is a major issue, and everyone on the team was genuinely lovely and kind. I think I simply expected the experience to feel a little more effortless and attentive at a Michelin-starred restaurant. The food absolutely deserves the praise, and I would happily come back to Corima, particularly to try the à la carte menu. I just wish the service and communication had been a little more refined and had made us feel slightly more looked after, because with food this good, that would have made the evening exceptional.

review_text:
I liked the room, which is annoying in retrospect. It was small, a little cramped, and full of the kind of references I grew up around in family restaurants. For a minute it felt quaint, familiar, like somebody’s actual kitchen. The meal did not survive that impression.

We had come for the fusion, that New York meeting of Hispanic and Chinese food, which is hardly a wild idea in this city. You would think someone in the building could talk about it. The waitress could not. Questions got hesitant, flummoxed half-answers, with no opinion and no sense of what was worth ordering. She set the plates down and left. Water was not refilled. A premade iced tea and a straw took about ten minutes. We were in the back booth by the bathroom, along one narrow walkway, so there was nowhere for her to pretend she was not passing us. She did, ten or twelve times, without a word, clearly clocking whether we were done. In a room that small, a stare is not subtle. The attention arrived for the exit and never for the meal. It felt scrutinized, and a little discriminatory.

The portions were generous for the price, and that is the only credit I will give. The food was greasy, overcooked, and mushy, oversalted and still underseasoned, with a gamey edge that belonged to neither tradition. The broccoli beside the sesame chicken was the best thing on the table, which is a miserable thing to have to admit. Everything else tasted like a five-minute search for the dish it was supposed to be. A bastardization. The drinks were the same failure in a glass: too tart and sour, or so sweet the fruit had disappeared.

I can speak for the Chinese side. The people with me can speak for the Hispanic side. None of us took this as gospel, and none of us were impressed. This city already has rooms that love both cuisines, and rooms that fuse them without embarrassing either one. This was the neighborhood worn as a costume. An overrated cash grab, with none of the love and none of the craft. I would not go back.

review_text:
I had heard really great things about this place and I was excited to try it on my last trip to New York, unfortunately, my experience was not great.

The food was actually really good—really decent portions, and some great vegan/vegetarian options. My main issue with my experience was the service and the atmosphere.

I was dining solo for brunch on a Sunday (a few weeks ago now) and noted that the patio and indoor seating were not full. I asked to sit on the patio if they had the space and the hostess was very short with me. She brought me out to this one patio table that was completely cut off from the rest of the tables, it had no umbrella and instead of regular chairs it had these little stools. It was at least 10 feet away from the other tables, on the opposite side of the door they use when delivering food to the patio. I want to note that the other patio seats were not full, and there were a number of additional options for me to be seated. I wouldn’t have minded the weird placement of the table if I were not dining solo—it seemed like a strange choice to seat the solo diner in the far corner of the patio (it honestly didn’t even feel like it was part of the patio, I might as well have been eating on the sidewalk).

The waitress was only polite when it came time to pay the bill. She seemed annoyed when I ordered my coffee first and needed another minute with the food menu.

About halfway through my meal, I wanted to ask to move inside since the fully exposed dunce corner seat was in direct sunlight and giving me a sunburn. I didn’t get the chance, since the waitress didn’t return for another 20 minutes or so. I just asked for the bill.

Since I’ve been a waitress, I tipped her well (i’m not a monster who doesn’t tip, even if the service sucks), which was the point of the interaction I got a brief smile, followed by her quickly leaving.

Honestly, I have a lot of patience for bad service usually, and I found the service in New York to be extremely courteous and lovely aside from this one experience. I just haven’t been able to get this meal out of my head since I ate there some weeks ago now.

I echo what some other commenters have said regarding the service. I think some training is needed, and perhaps adding another table to that very sad seating area where I was placed.

I absolutely love Dudley’s! I come here at least once a month, and it has easily become one of my favorite restaurants over the past 2–3 years. The food, service, and atmosphere are consistently great, and I’ve introduced so many friends to this place.

That being said, I think being such a regular customer allows me to offer some honest feedback.

On one occasion, I found a hair wrapped around my pancake after I had already covered it in syrup and was about to take my first bite. Of course, it was disappointing, but the staff handled it well, replaced my meal, and took it off the bill. Clearly, it didn’t stop me from coming back!

My biggest frustration is the inability to make reservations in the morning. I completely understand how busy brunch can get, especially on weekends and holidays, but I wish there were some flexibility. I tried making a reservation for Mother’s Day because I wanted to bring my mom, but unfortunately, that wasn’t an option.

I also wanted to mention the menu changes following the renovations. The restaurant itself looks beautiful, and I appreciate the updates, but I genuinely miss the original steak frites. It used to be one of my favorite dishes on the menu! While I appreciate the addition of the smothered steak, the changes to the steak frites have been disappointing, and I’ve found myself coming in for dinner much less frequently because of it.

Despite these few critiques, I really do love Dudley’s. It’s a place I consistently return to, recommend to others, and genuinely enjoy supporting. I was just here yesterday and I’m already coming back today!

review_text:
What a fantastic spot! I walked past this upscale-looking stall at Essex Market and noticed they were serving food, but there was no menu posted. I asked the guy behind the counter, who I believe is the owner, what they had. He explained that they had recently reopened at this location in August.  They had been after closed for a while.   He ran through three menu options. They all sounded delicious, but I wasn’t particularly hungry.

Then another customer, who had just ordered, casually said, “The sandwiches are life-changing.”

Well, that got my attention! I had to try one, so I ordered the chicken on a biscuit. It came out piping hot and incredibly fresh. That first bite was unbelievable. I ended up eating the entire sandwich, and I am officially SOLD! I’m a convert. This place is something special!

Even more remarkable, they have a “pay what you wish” policy. It’s such a unique, generous concept, and I love everything about it.

After eating, I was so caught up in how good the sandwich was that I accidentally left my man bag behind. I didn’t realize it until I got home, more than 40 minutes away by subway. I called, but there was no answer, so I went back.

When I arrived, the owner greeted me with a huge smile and said, “I was waiting for you to come back!” He explained that he had tried to find me before I left. My bag was right there, with absolutely everything still inside.

This man is not only a fantastic cook but also an honest, genuinely good-hearted human being. That kind of integrity is something you don’t forget.

Please go visit this place! Try the chicken on a biscuit, experience the food for yourself, and pay what you feel it’s worth. I have a feeling you’ll agree that it’s worth a lot of money.

Amazing food, an incredible concept, and an owner with real character. Go support him!

review_text:
VICTORIA! was a wonderful place for us to host a private event! The mix of standing room, tables of different heights and sizes, and decor made for a great venue for a highly social three-hour cocktail reception. We had about 30 guests, but probably could have fit twice as many. They let us bring in our own catering, which was great for flexibility and managing overall cost of the event.

Rachel was such a great bartender! Was super nice and helpful with setup and cleanup of the food and other items we brought in for our event. And made great drinks too!

We booked 6-9pm on a Saturday night, and were offered a contract with a very reasonable minimum spend, with flexibility for whether we paid it ourselves or guests would be billed individually (or some combination of those two). Regular patrons were let in at 9, but we were all having so much fun that most of us hung around for much longer.

The bar was so easy to work with and our event went so well. I seriously recommend anyone consider it for a private event.

review_text:
This one honestly hurt my heart…

Y’all… this review hurts my heart to write because I am a Sweet Chick fan.

Not a “I tried it once” fan. A real fan.

I’ve been going to Sweet Chick since there was only one location in Brooklyn. I was literally traveling from Jersey to Brooklyn just for the food, the drinks, and the experience, and I never minded doing it because it was always worth it.

So when they opened the Ludlow Street location, I was excited because now I didn’t have to make the trip to Brooklyn every time I wanted my chicken and waffles.

Back then, Sweet Chick was an experience.

They had the big specials board with rotating waffles, desserts, and seasonal items. Their chicken and waffles never missed. I honestly can’t remember ever leaving disappointed.

So this review is really hard for me.

Back on June 26th, after work, my mom and I decided to grab dinner. I work in the LES, and she suggested Sweet Chick. I did tell her my brother Robert had gone recently and said it had changed a lot, but we figured we’d see for ourselves.

We got there around 9-ish.

The first thing we noticed…

It was HOT.

Not warm.

Hot.

Like, “why does it feel like a sauna in here?” hot.

We’ve had enough hot weather this summer, so walking into a restaurant with little to no air conditioning was honestly uncomfortable. We actually debated leaving before we even ordered, but decided to stick it out.

Unfortunately… it never got better.

The service also wasn’t what I remembered.

I’m really big on customer service, and Sweet Chick has always had amazing service whenever I’ve gone. This time it just felt different. The attentiveness wasn’t there, and the overall vibe just felt… off.

Even the menu has changed.

My mom used to love their kale salad, but now it’s made differently with things like dates, and she wasn’t interested in it anymore.

For drinks, my mom ordered an espresso martini, and unfortunately she really didn’t enjoy it. It was pretty bitter, and we couldn’t quite figure out what was off about it. If I’m ordering an espresso martini, I have certain expectations, and this one just didn’t hit for her.

I ordered the Queen of New York, and I actually really enjoyed my drink. No complaints there.

Now… the food.

I ordered the Maple Chipotle Chicken & Sweet Potato Waffle.

And this is where my heart really broke.

Years ago, when they first introduced the sweet potato waffle as a special, I remember it actually tasting like sweet potato.

This one…

Honestly just tasted like a regular waffle.

I kept looking for that sweet potato flavor, and it just wasn’t there.

The chicken itself was crispy and cooked well, but the maple chipotle sauce wasn’t evenly coated. Some bites were really good, while other pieces were dry because they barely had any sauce on them.

Another thing longtime Sweet Chick fans might notice is the butter service.

I remember getting three or four different flavored butters, each in their own little container.

This time we got two flavors together in one cup.

It’s a small thing, but it was one of those details that always made Sweet Chick feel special.

My mom ordered the Carolina BBQ Chicken with the Grilled Corn Waffle.

I’ll be fair—her waffle absolutely tasted like a corn waffle. I tried it, and it was really good.

She enjoyed her meal more than I did, although she also had a few pieces of chicken that weren’t evenly coated with sauce and were a little dry.

Overall, she thought it was okay.

And I think that’s really the word for this visit.

Okay.

Not terrible.

But not the Sweet Chick we remembered.

Maybe that’s why this visit hit me so hard.

When you’ve loved a place for years, you naturally compare it to what you know it can be.

I genuinely hope this was just an off night because I have so many great memories here, and I’d honestly love to come back one day and have the Sweet Chick experience that made me fall in love with it in the first place.

Because this restaurant has meant a lot to me over the years, and I’m rooting for it.

I really am.

The fries we ordered were crispy, but lukewarm.  The grits tasted like we got the bottom of the pan they were dry instead of creamy. I also wish they served real maple syrup instead. The waffles were decent, but overall I've definitely had much better chicken and waffles elsewhere.
I was really looking forward to this meal based on all the hype, so it was a big disappointment.

review_text:
I came to Raoul’s for a burger and left with a new favorite person in Manhattan.

Our waitress Amy is a professional comedian disguised as a waitress, and somehow also a professional waitress. Every order came out right, nothing sat empty, and she checked on us with the kind of instinct usually reserved for golden retrievers and mothers of newborns. Great service is rare. Great service from someone who is funnier than your friends is something i didn't know existed until now. Sorry Jamie and Maddie.

As for the food, Raoul’s clearly knows it has to keep up with her, and it does. The au poivre burger was so good i briefly considered proposing to it: peppery, rich, cooked exactly right. We split the creme brûlée pancake, which is what would happen if a French pastry chef and a Waffle House employee had a sloppy one night stand. Rich, custardy, and gone way too fast.

Go for the burger. Stay for the pancake. But whatever you do, ask for Amy. Five stars, and that's only because the scale stops there. Don’t ask for a guinness though or you may get laughed out of town. Cheers.

The stuffy attitudes and loud music made a tiny space feel even smaller.

As for the food itself: except for the burger, the entire menu lacked the same finesse. I am currently nursing soda water and anti-acid trying to clean up the disaster that was the chicken dish. The menu says it's chicken, but if you close your eyes, you'll swear you're eating two breast-sized pieces of garlic. That was the only flavor which was odd because they promised salsa verde, which they said was actually an herb medley. I indeed saw the greens but I couldn't taste them or the chicken. Just garlic. Mountains and mountains of garlic.

The French soup was exciting at first bite but unfortunately disappointed thanks to the cheese atop which not bubbly, not golden, but subtly burnt as though it was sprinkled with cinders. The special ravioli was soaked in an orange lemon sauce that would have been more appropriate for vanilla ice cream. Cocktails were tiny, and the lemonade had an interesting lemon to sugar ratio: all sugar, a bit of lemon, and a rogue seed. Hey, at least it was made in house.

This restaurant is great if you don't really care for good tasting food and need somewhere to sit for no more than 60 minutes.

review_text:
An unforgettable experience in New York. And that says a lot considering the incredible number of dining and entertainment options Manhattan has to offer.
This is a place where you can enjoy outstanding food while being immersed in a truly unique atmosphere. The menu is not large, but it changes regularly, which makes the experience feel fresh and special.
During my visit, I chose the pan-seared duck confit, braised beef short rib, and crème brûlée for dessert. I also tried the Espresso-A-Go-Go cocktail, which was excellent and a perfect way to start the evening. Every dish was beautifully presented, served at the right time, and absolutely delicious. The portions were generous enough to fully appreciate the flavors without feeling overwhelming.
What makes this place truly exceptional, however, is the atmosphere and the show itself. The organizers have managed to create an intimate and cozy setting in a relatively small space, making every guest feel like part of the performance rather than just a spectator.
The performers are incredibly talented, charismatic, and full of energy. Their connection with the audience is effortless, and that energy spreads throughout the room, creating a genuinely memorable experience.
The price is fixed and includes a cocktail, appetizer, main course, and dessert. It is certainly not inexpensive, but in my opinion, it is worth every cent considering the quality of both the food and the entertainment.
Overall, this was one of the most memorable evenings I have had in New York. If you enjoy great food, live performances, and unique experiences, I highly recommend adding this place to your list.

review_text:
I celebrated my birthday at Estela, a one Michelin starred restaurant tucked away in a small, cozy space. I had high expectations coming in, but unfortunately, most of the dishes left me feeling underwhelmed.

They started us off with sourdough bread and olives, and surprisingly, the bread was one of my favorite things of the night. Fresh and warm, with a crunchy crust and a soft, doughy interior. Simple but so good.

Endive Salad: The highlight of the meal! Probably the second best salad I’ve ever had in my life. Served with walnuts, anchovies, and citrus juice, the combination was perfectly balanced and packed with flavor. I could honestly come back just for this. A MUST order!

Fried Arroz Negro: Essentially squid ink fried rice, but there was barely any squid, if any at all. The dish felt underwhelming and was missing the seafood element I was hoping for.

Ricotta Dumplings: Pretty good overall, served with thinly sliced mushrooms. Nothing mind blowing, but a solid dish.

Golden Tilefish: Unfortunately, this was dry and overcooked, very disappointing.

Pork Collar: Another disappointment. The pork was noticeably undercooked, and the dish fell short in both execution and flavor.

The portions are on the smaller side, almost like tapas, so the bill adds up quickly without feeling particularly satisfying. I really wanted to love Estela, especially given its Michelin star and reputation, but aside from the endive salad and sourdough bread, the meal didn’t leave much of an impression.

While the store itself is fairly small and unglamorous, the food is worthwhile. I plan to return to try more menu items sometime in the near future!

Great food, fantastic flavors, crispy textures done right, incredible desserts, and prices that make you want to come back and try even more of the menu. review_text:
Visited on September 8th

Casino is a beautifully sexy and elegant restaurant, perfectly situated in a pocket of the Lower East Side where time feels delightfully suspended. It sits in one of the few corners of Manhattan that hasn't been homogenized by rapid gentrification. Here, the true spirit of New York's melting pot remains entirely intact. Looking out, you witness a vibrant crossroads of cultures--a rich diversity that is beautifully mirrored in both the neighborhood's people and the exceptional variety of its culinary landscape.

This was my second visit to Casino, and I was eager to return after being blown away by the food, service, and decor the first time. On this second visit, it felt like walking into an entirely different world--in the best way possible. The dining room transported us straight into a 1940s movie, offering a smoky, sexy, and elegant ambiance (minus the actual smoke). My husband and I were celebrating our wedding anniversary, and the team perfectly set the mood by accommodating our request for a red banquette. Our waitress was incredibly warm, friendly, and offered excellent recommendations. When I asked for wine pairings, she seamlessly transitioned us to Daniel, the sommelier. His recommendations were absolutely beautiful, pairing flawlessly with both my appetizer and entree. My only slight disappointment was that he sent our waitress over to pour and sample the wine rather than presenting it himself.  He did drop by at the end of our meal but it was bittersweet.

My husband and I had a mixed culinary experience here, marked by some disappointing appetizers but truly exceptional pasta dishes.

The Grilled Prawns with Calabrian Chili: We were both pretty underwhelmed by this dish. It lacked the vibrant punch we were expecting.  The Funghi Fritti (Tempura Battered Mushrooms): Honestly, these were awful. They were literally rock-hard, and no amount of lemon aioli or Calabrian chili sauce was going to rehydrate them. The Main Courses: Bucatini with Clams: My husband opted for this and thought it was delicious. The sauce was absolutely gorgeous; his only minor critique was that he wished there had been a bit more of it.  I ordered the Tagliatelle Bolognese: This was the absolute star of the night. It was, without a doubt, the best Bolognese I have ever had in my life.

We highly recommend this hidden gem!

P.S. The hostess checked on every table except ours.

Simple ingredients prepared well. Fresh crunchy veggies against a mouse-like tofu lathered with a very creamy  and lightly spicy sauce.

Imagine childhood lap cheung (sausage) turn into a jam paste so you can dip your toast aka fried curler in it. It’s only 4.5 because I like my yaotiew less fried/more airy inside

Creamy again, but this time, a burst of garlic (and ginger) and other herbs/spices to round out the flavor profile. Hints of sweetness involved

The crispy skin of roasted pork combined with the fattiness of duck, but the heavy paste-like sauce absorbs it and prepares it to stick well against the paper-thin wrap
5. Mango coconut pudding with grapefruit 4/5
Mango— deep flavors
Coconut— light flavors
Grapefruit— the grapefruit is too tart against the smooth mango. Either less grapefruit or a different fruit

It's probably because I'm French (the country of origin of the crêpe, born in Brittany) that reading the reviews, almost all of them rave about this establishment, surprises me somewhat...

The PUBLIC hotel is incredible, I believe it truly caters to all needs. We stayed in Queen Hi-Floor rooms which were a perfect size for a six night trip.

The hotel is a great location, in-between all the major shops of 5th Avenue etc and downtown Manhattan. Expect to be walking a lot in NYC :)

Unfortunately on our last night, one of our party had a medical emergency and being from the UK and unfamiliar with the US medical system, the hotel staff were incredible in helping us, they accommodated all of our needs and were so supportive in the midst of a crisis. I especially want to mention Lasandra, Jonathan, and both reception teams who were there on the evening of the 15th and morning of the 16th. I wouldn't have been able to navigate such a difficult situation without their help and I will be forever grateful they were there.

On the note of your staff, I also had the pleasure of meeting Ella and Solana, in both the rooftop bar and the downstairs bar behind the pool table. They were so hospitable, and such lovely girls!! Unfortunately I had the unpleasant experience of running into quite a rude and aggressive patron of the downstairs bar, behind the pool table. From what I could understand this man was not a guest of the hotel and was being incredibly rude to bar tender on duty that night and her bar back (I didn't catch their names). I complained about this behaviour to the bar manager that night, I believe their name is Jay and said I would like this person removed for being so disgustingly rude to their staff there, of which Jay refused to do. I understand situations like that need to be handled carefully, however from my own observations I could tell the staff behind the bar that night were uncomfortable with this man and I believe Jay did not look out for his staff appropriately and this should be addressed internally.

Overall, my family and I had the most incredible time in NYC and our stay at The PUBLIC hotel was everything we had hoped for and more.

We will be returning.

Kindest, Stella

review_text:
**Heavy on style, light on amenities**

Everything at the Public screams "Design," and some of it is genuinely good. Our corner loft room was spacious, with a beautiful exposed concrete ceiling and dramatic views. But the yellow, semi-transparent glass toilet enclosure offered little privacy, and closet space was tight for one of the largest room categories. There's no room service, no turndown service, no coffee machine and no minibar, just a small, empty fridge.

The WeWork-style lobby is open to the public and packed with laptop-wielding hipsters, leaving little or no room for hotel guests, and there's nowhere else to lounge. The cocktail bar was closed for two of our four days. That left the rooftop bar, which is pleasant, weather permitting, if you can ignore the sour staff.

There's no real restaurant either, just a ground-floor deli and breakfast bar with equally unhappy staff. The continental breakfast included in the rate is meager: drip coffee or tea, orange or grapefruit juice, and one item such as a croissant. Sandwiches are extra. At an average of around $800 a night, you'd think they could throw in a cappuccino, or keep their dignity and not include breakfast at all.

Most of the time there is only one person at the reception desk, which means long queues. This was at its worst when we came back for the luggage we'd left with the hotel after checking out. The unfriendly receptionist told us no one was available to fetch bags from the luggage room and that we'd have to do it ourselves. So six groups of guests trooped up to the second floor to find an office she'd pointed us to, where someone could finally take us to the luggage room.

If you're willing to spend $800 a night, there are far better hotels in New York that offer the same design fix but know a great deal more about amenities and customer service than the Public.

My stay at PUBLIC Hotel left a lot to be desired, starting with a frustrating check-in experience. Despite arriving at 3:10 PM (past the 3:00 PM check-in time), I was unable to use the iPad check-in because I hadn't received a room number yet.

When I spoke to the front desk, I was told my room wasn’t ready because the previous guest had a late check-out, and that my personal request for robes and slippers—which I had submitted three weeks in advance—was causing an additional delay.

When I asked for an ETA, I was simply told to come back in 20 minutes. I returned around 3:30pm and spoke with another staff member who gave a vague answer. Given the inconvenient delay that nearly made me late for an uptown reservation at 5pm, I asked if a late check-out could be accommodated for my departure day. I was told they couldn't approve it at the desk and I’d have to call down later. No gesture or accommodation was offered to alleviate the inconvenience, making for a poor first impression.

To top it off, when I finally got to the room, the robes and slippers I requested three weeks prior were missing. When I asked about them later that evening, I was told they were completely out of slippers, though we did eventually receive the robes.

On a positive note, the room itself was clean. However, noise traveled easily through the door and you could hear people talking in the hall, making it less than peaceful.

Ultimately, I’ve had much better service and hospitality at other New York City hotels, and unfortunately, I will not be returning.

review_text:
I attended an event here tonight and was accused of stealing FREE merchandise.
When I walked in, a friendly staff member at the name tag table encouraged me and other attendees to check out the stickers at the table perpendicular to hers. I watched several people ahead of me take merchandise from that table, and when it was my turn, I did the same. I want to emphasize this was FREE merchandise — just like the food and matcha drinks being handed out elsewhere at the event, which nobody else was questioned about.
As I zipped up my bag, a staff member approached me and said, "I was not allowed to put that in my bag." I was confused and asked, "You mean the FREE gear we were just told we could take?" He replied, "I have to go check in to see if YOU can have that."
I was understandably offended. I had just watched other people take the same items, and I'd been explicitly told it was for everyone. I waited while he went to "verify" something that had already been made clear. He came back and confirmed, with total confidence, what I already knew.
What made it worse: I recognized this same staff member from earlier, stationed by the door. When another guest in line asked him why there were two lines, he said he didn't know and pointed down the block to someone else as the "point person."
Being singled out and accused like this put a real damper on an event I'd been looking forward to. I'm not writing this review because I was mistaken for a moment — I'm writing it because instead of a simple apology, he doubled down and made me feel like I was in the wrong. In hindsight, I should've escalated it on the spot, but the staff already looked overwhelmed managing the line, and I didn't want to make a scene over stickers.
I enjoyed the rest of the event and didn't let his weaponized incompetence ruin my night. But I won't be back ,  my loss, I guess.

review_text:
I liked the room, which is annoying in retrospect. It was small, a little cramped, and full of the kind of references I grew up around in family restaurants. For a minute it felt quaint, familiar, like somebody’s actual kitchen. The meal did not survive that impression.

We had come for the fusion, that New York meeting of Hispanic and Chinese food, which is hardly a wild idea in this city. You would think someone in the building could talk about it. The waitress could not. Questions got hesitant, flummoxed half-answers, with no opinion and no sense of what was worth ordering. She set the plates down and left. Water was not refilled. A premade iced tea and a straw took about ten minutes. We were in the back booth by the bathroom, along one narrow walkway, so there was nowhere for her to pretend she was not passing us. She did, ten or twelve times, without a word, clearly clocking whether we were done. In a room that small, a stare is not subtle. The attention arrived for the exit and never for the meal. It felt scrutinized, and a little discriminatory.

The portions were generous for the price, and that is the only credit I will give. The food was greasy, overcooked, and mushy, oversalted and still underseasoned, with a gamey edge that belonged to neither tradition. The broccoli beside the sesame chicken was the best thing on the table, which is a miserable thing to have to admit. Everything else tasted like a five-minute search for the dish it was supposed to be. A bastardization. The drinks were the same failure in a glass: too tart and sour, or so sweet the fruit had disappeared.

I can speak for the Chinese side. The people with me can speak for the Hispanic side. None of us took this as gospel, and none of us were impressed. This city already has rooms that love both cuisines, and rooms that fuse them without embarrassing either one. This was the neighborhood worn as a costume. An overrated cash grab, with none of the love and none of the craft. I would not go back.

review_text:
La Pizza Napoli is a hidden gem. Their margarita pizza is amazing. I love their pizza by the slice option, and genuinely affordable prices for being in Manhattan. But the thing that stood out the most to me was how lovely the staff were. They took such excellent care of me, and were genuinely so patient and understanding with all customers. The owner cares very deeply about his store, and it shows. Overall, I’d make it a point to visit this pizza shop every time I happen to be in the Big Apple purely because of how wonderful not only the food is, but also how incredibly kind, thoughtful, and caring the staff is.

I wish the owner much success, and hope he expands to more locations.
